title: Unit 3: Land-Based Empires

topics.name: Empires expand
covers: The development of the Manchu, Mughal, Ottoman, and Safavid empires

topics.name: Administering empires
covers: How rulers of empires maintained their power

guide.title: Unit 3: Land-Based Empires: review guide
guide.intro: From about 1450 to 1750, large land-based empires such as the Ottoman, Safavid, Mughal, and Qing expanded with gunpowder weapons and governed huge, diverse populations. This unit covers how they grew, how rulers kept power, and how religion both united and divided them.

sections.title: Empires expand
body: The Ottomans used large cannons to take Constantinople in 1453 and later expanded into the Balkans, the Middle East, and North Africa. The Safavids, founded by Shah Ismail in 1501, ruled Persia; the Mughals, founded by Babur in 1526, ruled most of South Asia; and the Manchus conquered Ming China in 1644, founding the Qing dynasty, which later expanded into Mongolia, Tibet, and Xinjiang.

Historians often call the Ottoman, Safavid, and Mughal states “gunpowder empires” because firearms and artillery helped them expand and centralize. Russia also expanded across Siberia, driven partly by the fur trade.
points: Know the founding dates and regions of the main empires.
Gunpowder weapons favored states that could afford cannons and trained infantry.

sections.title: How rulers kept power
body: Rulers built bureaucracies and recruited loyal elites. The Ottoman devshirme took Christian boys from the Balkans, converted them, and trained them as Janissary soldiers or officials. The Mughals relied on zamindars to collect land taxes, and the Ottomans used tax farming. Qing emperors kept the Confucian examination system while requiring Han Chinese men to wear the Manchu queue hairstyle.

Rulers also used monumental architecture (the Taj Mahal, the Palace of Versailles) and court rituals to display power. Louis XIV kept nobles at Versailles, and the Tokugawa shoguns required lords to spend alternate years in Edo; both policies kept powerful elites close and under watch.
points: Ask how each method helped legitimize or consolidate power.
Comparison questions often ask about methods shared across empires.

sections.title: Belief systems in empires
body: Religion legitimized rulers and shaped conflict. The Sunni Ottomans and Shia Safavids fought repeatedly, as at the Battle of Chaldiran (1514). In Europe, Martin Luther's challenge to the Catholic Church in 1517 began the Protestant Reformation; the Catholic Counter-Reformation, including the Council of Trent, responded.

In South Asia, Sikhism emerged from the teachings of Guru Nanak, blending elements of Hinduism and Islam. The Mughal emperor Akbar promoted tolerance and abolished the jizya, a tax on non-Muslims, while Aurangzeb later reimposed it. The Ottoman millet system let religious communities manage many of their own affairs.
points: Religious policy was a political tool for winning or controlling subjects.
Religious splits often matched political rivalries.

example.prompt: Explain one similarity in how the Ottoman and Mughal rulers kept control of diverse populations.
example.solution: Both granted some religious toleration to large non-Muslim populations (the Ottoman millet system; Akbar's abolition of the jizya) while relying on loyal elites and tax collectors, which reduced resistance and kept revenue flowing.

misconceptions: “The gunpowder empires were all ruled by the same dynasty.”
Ottomans, Safavids, and Mughals were separate dynasties, often rivals.
The Qing were Manchus who conquered Ming China and ruled a mostly Han population.
Non-Muslims often paid special taxes and faced limits even under tolerant rulers.
Gunpowder came from China and spread across Eurasia.

passages.title: Source A: An interpretation of the expansion of land-based empires
text: “In 1453 the Ottoman sultan Mehmed II brought massive cannons against the walls of Constantinople, which had protected the Byzantine capital for a thousand years. The city fell, and it became the Ottoman capital. In the decades that followed, new dynasties built empires across Asia. Shah Ismail founded the Safavid state in Persia in 1501, and Babur, a descendant of Timur, defeated the sultan of Delhi in 1526 and founded the Mughal Empire. Farther east, the Manchus from the northeast seized Beijing in 1644 and founded the Qing dynasty. These states differed in language and culture, but the Ottomans, Safavids, and Mughals all invested heavily in firearms and artillery.”

passages.title: Source B: An interpretation of imperial administration
text: “Rulers of vast empires needed loyal servants who owed everything to the throne. The Ottomans took Christian boys from Balkan villages through the devshirme, converted them to Islam, and trained the most able as Janissary infantry or palace administrators. In Mughal India, zamindars collected land taxes and passed a share to the emperor. European and Asian rulers alike worked to tame their nobles. Louis XIV of France required great nobles to live at his palace at Versailles, where their status depended on his favor, while in Japan the Tokugawa shoguns made regional lords spend alternate years in the capital, Edo. Across these empires, the Ottoman millet system let Christian and Jewish communities run many of their own affairs.”
passages.attribution: Interpretation written for StudySprint by its editors. It summarizes widely held historical views and is not a quotation from any published historian.
passages.licenseOrRights: Original text written for StudySprint; it is not taken or adapted from any College Board exam.

passages.title: Source C: An interpretation of religion and power
text: “Religion was both a source of legitimacy and a cause of conflict. The Safavid shahs made Shia Islam the official faith of Persia, while their Ottoman rivals championed Sunni Islam; in 1514 the two clashed at Chaldiran. In Europe, Martin Luther's 1517 attack on the sale of indulgences split Western Christianity, and Catholic and Protestant rulers fought for more than a century. In South Asia, Guru Nanak taught a devotion to one God that drew on both Hindu and Islamic traditions, giving rise to Sikhism. The Mughal emperor Akbar welcomed scholars of many faiths and ended the jizya, a tax on non-Muslims. His great-grandson Aurangzeb restored it in 1679.”
passages.attribution: Interpretation written for StudySprint by its editors. It summarizes widely held historical views and is not a quotation from any published historian.

passages.title: Source D: An interpretation of the Qing and Russian empires
text: “The Manchu rulers of the Qing dynasty faced a problem: they were a small conquering minority ruling hundreds of millions of Han Chinese. They kept the Confucian civil service examinations and employed Han officials, but they required Han men to wear the Manchu queue hairstyle as a sign of submission. Under the Kangxi and Qianlong emperors, the Qing added Taiwan, Mongolia, Tibet, and Xinjiang, roughly doubling the territory of the Ming. At the same time, Russia expanded east across Siberia, drawn by furs that could be sold at high prices. Supporting armies and officials across such distances strained every empire, and rulers experimented with ways of collecting revenue.”
